opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that we're still figuring it out. For a while the dominant intuition was that you'd just keep scaling one big general model and it would get better at everything, and to a surprising degree that's held up. Generality has been really powerful, because skills transfer in ways you don't expect: getting better at code makes the model better at reasoning in general, and so on.

But I do think you'll see specialization emerge at a few different levels. Inside the model, things like mixture-of-experts already give you a kind of soft specialization, where different parts of the network get routed different kinds of inputs. We don't fully control what those experts learn, and interpretability work suggests the divisions often don't map neatly onto human categories like "the math expert" or "the French expert." It's messier than that.

Then there's specialization at the system level, which I think is where a lot of the practical action will be. You might have a very capable general model acting as an orchestrator, delegating to smaller, faster, cheaper models for subtasks where you don't need the full horsepower. That's partly an economics question. If something runs millions of times a day, you want it efficient.

And then there's the agentic side. As models do longer-horizon tasks, you may want different instances with different contexts, tools, or roles working together, almost like a team. Whether that ends up as genuinely different architectures or the same underlying model wearing different hats is an open question. My guess is it's mostly the latter for a while, because the base capabilities are so valuable to share.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming specialization means narrowness. The most useful specialized systems will probably still sit on top of a very broad foundation, because the edge cases in any domain require general world knowledge and judgment. So it's less "many small expert models" and more "a strong generalist core with specialized structure layered around it."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it's going to look different than people expect. The intuition a lot of folks have is that specialization means you'll have a legal model and a medical model and a coding model, each trained from scratch on its own corpus. I actually think that's mostly wrong, because so much of what makes a model good at any one of those things is general capability. The reasoning, the ability to follow instructions, the world knowledge. If you strip that out to make a narrow model, you usually end up with something worse at the narrow task, not better.

So where I think specialization actually shows up is more in a few other places. One is at the level of the architecture itself, things like mixture of experts, where you have a single model but different parts of the network light up for different kinds of inputs. That's specialization, but it's learned, it's emergent, and the model is deciding how to route rather than us deciding ahead of time. And I think that trend continues. The model figures out its own internal division of labor better than we would.

The second place is post-training. You can take the same base model and shape it pretty substantially with fine-tuning and reinforcement learning toward a particular job. That's much cheaper than training a new model, and you retain all the general capability underneath. At Anthropic a lot of what we do with Claude is really about that layer, getting the model to be good at the things people actually want to do, like coding or long agentic tasks, without losing the generalist.

And then the third place, and maybe the most interesting one, is at the system level rather than the model level. You have a big, highly capable model that acts as the orchestrator, and it delegates to smaller or cheaper models for subtasks, or to tools, or to other instances of itself. The specialization is in the scaffolding and the workflow, not necessarily in the weights. I think that's where a lot of the near-term value is going to come from, because it lets you match the cost of the compute to the difficulty of the piece of work.

The one thing I'd push back on is the idea that scaling and specialization are in tension. I think they're complementary. The bigger and more general the frontier models get, the more they become the thing you specialize from, and the more useful it is to have good tooling for doing that. So I expect to see both at once: a small number of very general frontier models, and a huge ecosystem of specialized behavior built on top of them.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of ways this could play out. One is specialization within a model, where different parts of the network become good at different kinds of tasks, and you learn how to route work to those parts. The other is specialization at the system level: you have multiple models with different capabilities, costs, and latencies, and something decides which one to use.

The interesting tension is that generality is itself really valuable. Being good at coding might help you reason through a problem that doesn’t initially look like a coding problem. So if you specialize too aggressively, you could lose some of that transfer.

My guess is we’ll see a combination: a broadly capable model coordinating more specialized components. But I’m uncertain how much of that structure we’ll explicitly design and how much will emerge through training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll probably see specialization at a few different levels. You can have a general-purpose model that gets really good at a particular domain through additional training. But you can also have a system made up of different models, where some component decides which model to call for a particular task.

The interesting question is where that specialization should live. Do you want it inside one big model, or do you want separate models with different capabilities and different costs? I suspect we’ll see both. If you’re doing something relatively straightforward, you’d like to use a small, fast model. If you hit a really difficult problem, you want to spend more compute.

And I wouldn’t assume that the boundaries will line up neatly with human professions. You might get specialization around particular kinds of reasoning or particular parts of a workflow. A lot of this will come down to what’s easiest to train and what actually works reliably.
